body.axialTiltNote: Earth's obliquity to its orbital plane (the ecliptic).
body.datum: GEBCO: 0 m is mean sea level.
body.dayLengthNote: Earth's sidereal day. The solar day is 24 h; the sidereal one is what the Coriolis deflection actually depends on.
body.rotationDirectionNote: Prograde: seen from above the north pole, Earth turns anticlockwise.

climate._note: Overrides for js/climate.js, which holds the schema (default, physical/empirical, range, meaning). Missing entries take the default; unknown ones are ignored. Fitted by a program, never by hand, against this world's own satellite photograph: the photo is classified pixel by pixel into vegetation, bare ground and snow, and the model is scored against that -- globally, per region (so one continent's excess cannot pay for another's shortfall), and at twenty named places.
climate._paletteNote: Measured from this world's own photograph, not chosen: each swatch is the mean of the pixels at one end of a class's real range -- the greenest vegetated ground, the brightest hot bare ground, the darkest cold bare ground, the veg/bare transition, and snow.

climateSets._note: Named climate sets. Each one lists only what it changes from the `climate` block above, which in turn lists only what it changes from the schema defaults in js/climate.js -- so the twenty fitted numbers are written down exactly once and a set that moves one number is one line. Resolved separately, so a set naming a retired parameter is reported and skipped without spoiling the others. Only one set today: the 寒冷/温暖 sets it shipped with were nothing but a different meanTemperatureC, and that is now a slider, so keeping them would have been the same control twice on a panel the user has already said is too tall. The mechanism stays for the stage that keeps a spread of genuinely different candidates.

teacher._note: What this world's surface really looks like, for the climate model to be scored against. Built by tools/build_teacher.py; see that file for what each class is sourced from and how far to trust it. One byte per cell: 0 sea, 1 sea ice, 2 vegetation, 3 arid, 4 land ice. Adding a past or future era means adding an entry here and a builder in that tool -- nothing else in the project knows how many eras there are.

sources.landSea: GEBCO_2026 ice-surface grid (the same committed raster the globe's shape uses)
sources.landIce: Natural Earth 1:10m glaciated areas + Antarctic ice shelves (public domain)
sources.vegetation: Blue Marble surface photograph, by colour (G > R)
sources.arid: Blue Marble surface photograph, by colour (G <= R)
sources.seaIce: Blue Marble surface photograph: bright, colour-neutral water. The weakest layer -- a composite image, not a measured extent.

terrain.source: GEBCO_2026 Grid (ice surface elevation), 15 arc-second, via CEDA
